\section[alcanzar]{alcanzar — to reach, to catch up with}

\label{lesson:ES-C573-alcanzar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to develop, then the Spanish for to overcome.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: alcanzar}
\textbf{alcanzar} — \textquotedblleft{}to reach, to catch up with\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Después de tres horas alcanzamos al grupo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After three hours we caught up with the group.}
\end{quote}

It takes \emph{c} before \emph{e}: \emph{alcancé}. \emph{Alcanzar un objetivo} — to achieve a goal.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{alcanzar} is usually traced to spoken Latin \emph{*incalciāre} 'to follow at the heels' (EtymDB), built on \emph{calx} 'heel'. To catch up is to be on someone's heels.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{alcanzar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{alcanzar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{alcanzar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to develop, then the Spanish for to overcome, then say \emph{alcanzar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does alcanzar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To reach, to catch up with\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fracasar]{fracasar — to fail}

\label{lesson:ES-C573-fracasar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to overcome, then the Spanish for to reach.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fracasar}
\textbf{fracasar} — \textquotedblleft{}to fail\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El proyecto fracasó por falta de dinero.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The project failed for lack of money.}
\end{quote}

Used for plans and projects; to fail an exam is \emph{suspender}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fracasar} was borrowed from Italian \emph{fracassare} 'to smash, to shatter' (EtymDB). A plan that fails is smashed.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fracasar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{fracasar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to overcome, then the Spanish for to reach, then say \emph{fracasar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does fracasar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To fail\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el fracaso]{el fracaso — the failure}

\label{lesson:ES-C573-fracaso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to reach, then the Spanish for to fail.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el fracaso}
\textbf{el fracaso} — \textquotedblleft{}the failure\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La película fue un fracaso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The film was a failure.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fracaso} comes from Italian \emph{fracasso} 'a crash, a smash' (EtymDB), from \emph{fracassare} 'to smash to pieces'.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[sufrir]{sufrir — to suffer; to undergo}

\label{lesson:ES-C573-sufrir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to fail, then the Spanish for the failure.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sufrir}
\textbf{sufrir} — \textquotedblleft{}to suffer; to undergo\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Sufrió un accidente de tráfico.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He was in a road accident.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Sufrir un accidente} — to have an accident. \emph{Sufrir de} — to suffer from.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sufrir} comes from Latin \emph{sufferre} 'to bear up under' (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{sub} 'under' and \emph{ferre} 'to carry', usually through a spoken Latin form \emph{*sufferīre}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[resultar]{resultar — to turn out, to prove to be}

\label{lesson:ES-C573-resultar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the failure, then the Spanish for to suffer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: resultar}
\textbf{resultar} — \textquotedblleft{}to turn out, to prove to be\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El examen resultó muy fácil.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The exam turned out to be very easy.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Resultar herido} — to be injured: \emph{Dos personas resultaron heridas.}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{resultar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{resultāre} 'to spring back, to rebound' (EtymDB), built on \emph{resilīre} 'to leap back', from \emph{salīre} 'to leap' (Lewis \& Short). A result is what springs back from an action.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
